results.content: 6 Chapter 1 Introduction 2 Supervised- & Semi-supervised Deep Learning for Anomaly Detection in Brain MRI 2.1 Deﬁnition of Brain Anomaly Detection in a Supervised Context In their survey of traditional anomaly detection papers for medical image analysis, Taboada-Crispi et al.[94] differentiate between three different types of anomaly detection, based on degress of prior knowledge: a) methods completely devoid of prior knowledge, b) approaches which know alone about normality and c) techniques which utilize knowledge about both normal and abnormal cases. 3.2 Unsupervised Deep Representation Learning & Deep Generative Models In brain imaging, UAD has seen a wide array of methods, ranging from clustering-techniques based on unsupervised representation learning with AEs to the recent wave of distribution modeling with deep generative modeling frameworks such as Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) and hybrids thereof. Authors: Christoph Baur, Robert Graf, Benedikt Wiestler, Shadi Albarqouni, Nassir Navab Title: “SteGANomaly: Inhibiting CycleGAN Steganography for Unsupervised Anomaly Detection in Brain MRI” In: Medical Image Computing and Computer Assisted Intervention–MICCAI 2020: 23rd International Conference, Lima, Peru, October 4–8, 2020, Proceedings, Part II 23 DOI: 3.3 GAN-based Anomaly Detection 29 3.4 Autoencoder-based Anomaly Detection 3.4.1 Concept and related work Fig. 3.5 Training and inference of AE-based models for UAS in image-space from reconstruction residuals (Source: [11]). The nature of AE-based models allows to directly project samples onto the lower-dimensional manifold z and to generate normal-looking reconstructions of abnormal data very efﬁciently in a single forward pass through the 30 Chapter 3 Unsupervised Deep Learning for Anomaly Detection in Brain MRI trained model. results.content: A Systematic Review of Foundation Models for Brain Imaging and Biomedical Research. A Systematic Review of Foundation Models for Brain Imaging and Biomedical Research. [[Literature Review] Foundation Models in Medical Imaging -- A Review and Outlook](/review/foundation-models-in-medical-imaging-a-review-and-outlook)[[Literature Review] Towards Generalisable Foundation Models for 3D Brain MRI](/review/towards-generalisable-foundation-models-for-3d-brain-mri)[[Literature Review] Brain Foundation Models with Hypergraph Dynamic Adapter for Brain Disease Analysis](/review/brain-foundation-models-with-hypergraph-dynamic-adapter-for-brain-disease-analysis)[[Literature Review] Exploring Zero-Shot Anomaly Detection with CLIP in Medical Imaging: Are We There Yet?](/review/exploring-zero-shot-anomaly-detection-with-clip-in-medical-imaging-are-we-there-yet)[[Literature Review] A Foundation Model for Brain Lesion Segmentation with Mixture of Modality Experts](/review/a-foundation-model-for-brain-lesion-segmentation-with-mixture-of-modality-experts). A Systematic Review of Foundation Models for Brain Imaging and Biomedical Research](/file? Foundation models (FMs), large neural networks pretrained on extensive and diverse datasets, offer significant potential in medical imaging, enabling robust performance with limited labeled data. Existing surveys often underrepresent or lack depth on the unique challenges of FMs in brain imaging, despite its critical role in neurological disease diagnosis using modalities like MRI, CT, and PET. Dataset diversity criteria for FMs include training on at least two imaging modalities, two different organs (including brain), or two different brain pathologies (e.g., brain tumor, vascular disease). After full-text assessment based on introducing a novel brain FM and evaluation on brain/head imaging, 86 research papers were included (34 from the initial search, 52 from augmentation). Notable early models include Genesis and Med3D (U-Net, CNNs), while recent influential models include MedSAM and LLaVA-Med. Architecturally, 63% of FMs are image-only, evenly split between 2D (57%) and 3D (51%) inputs, with some supporting both (5 models) or 4D multi-sequence inputs with missing modalities (11 models). 63% of FMs used datasets combining brain images with other organs. 2D datasets (e.g., ROCO, COSMOS 1050K) are often scrapped, multimodal (image-text), and cover multiple organs, including brain. Key innovations in highlighted models include: OE-VQA (autoregressive VQA), Med-VLP (knowledge injection in pre-training), Anomaly-CLIP (object-agnostic zero-shot anomaly detection), Med-PALMM (multi-modal, multi-task integration), MIU-VL (automated medical prompt generation), CLOPT (large-scale contrastive SSL on 100M+ images), PCRLv2 (pixel-level restoration, scale-aware SSL for 3D), MedLSAM (SAM adaptation with few-shot 3D localization), MoME (MoE for modality-specific experts, curriculum learning), BrainSegFounder (two-stage SSL for healthy anatomy then pathology), RadFM (large-scale multimodal dataset, generative approach, RadBench benchmark), MUMC (multi-objective pre-training for VQA).
